descriptions: A single hyperspectral pixel of the Asphalt class.
Reflectance is low to moderate across the 430-860 nm range.
Reflectance increases gradually from visible wavelengths toward 860 nm.
The spectrum is broadly flat with a slight convex curvature in the NIR.
No red-edge transition is present; the spectrum lacks vegetation features.
Variability arises from differences in age, moisture, and composition.
This pixel belongs to the Meadows class.
Reflectance is low in visible bands and high in near-infrared, giving a moderate overall level.
The spectral slope from visible to 860 nm is strongly positive.
A broad concave shape in visible bands transitions to convex curvature in the near-infrared.
Red-edge is present as a steep reflectance increase from red to near-infrared wavelengths.
Intra-class variation arises from moisture, chlorophyll content, and leaf senescence.
This is a single hyperspectral pixel of gravel.
Reflectance is generally moderate across the 430-860 nm range with variability.
Reflectance increases slightly from visible wavelengths toward 860 nm.
The spectral curve is broadly linear without pronounced curvature.
No red edge is present as gravel is non-vegetation.
Variation arises from mineral composition, moisture, and grain size.
This is a single hyperspectral pixel belonging to the Trees class.
Reflectance is generally low in visible bands and high in NIR, so overall medium to high.
Reflectance increases sharply from visible wavelengths toward 860 nm, producing a strong positive slope.
The broad curve is concave in visible bands and convex approaching 860 nm, with a smooth transition.
A distinct red-edge transition occurs, with a steep reflectance increase from red to near-infrared wavelengths.
Intra-class variation results from differences in canopy shadow, leaf moisture, and sub-pixel mixing.
A single pixel belongs to the Painted Metal Sheets class.
Reflectance is moderate to high across the 430-860 nm range, variable with paint color.
The spectrum is broadly flat or slightly increasing from visible to 860 nm.
The spectral curve is generally linear with possible minor convex or concave curvature.
No red-edge feature is present as this is a non-vegetation class.
Variation arises from paint color, aging, moisture, and sub-pixel mixing.
This pixel is classified as bare soil from its hyperspectral signature.
Reflectance is moderate across the 430-860 nm range, varying with soil composition.
A gradual positive slope from visible wavelengths to 860 nm is typical.
The spectrum shows a broad convex shape or monotonic increase without sharp transitions.
No red-edge is present; the spectrum lacks the sharp vegetation reflectance increase.
Variation arises from differences in moisture, organic matter, and mineral composition.
A single hyperspectral pixel of Bitumen.
Reflectance is low across the 430-860 nm range, typically under 10%.
Reflectance is nearly flat or very gradually increasing from visible to 860 nm.
No pronounced curvature; the spectrum is broadly linear or weakly concave upward.
Red edge is absent because Bitumen is not vegetation; no sharp transition around 700 nm.
Variation arises from surface aging, moisture content, and minor compositional differences.
This hyperspectral pixel belongs to the class Self-Blocking Bricks.
Reflectance is generally moderate, varying with brick color and surface condition.
Reflectance increases gradually from visible wavelengths toward 860 nm, with moderate slope.
The spectrum exhibits a broad convex shape, with gradual transitions and no sharp features.
No diagnostic red-edge is present; any inflection is weak and non-vegetation-like.
Spectral variation arises from differences in clay composition, firing, moisture, and surface aging.
This is a single hyperspectral pixel belonging to the Shadows class.
Reflectance is typically low across the 430 to 860 nm range.
The spectrum shows a broadly flat or slightly positive slope from visible to near-infrared.
No pronounced curvature; the spectral shape remains generally linear.
No diagnostic red-edge feature is present as shadows lack vegetation spectral signatures.
Intra-class variation arises from differing illumination levels and sub-pixel material mixing.
